old: They work under high pressure, and they have no valves.
new: They generally have thicker walls and higher pressures than veins; the aortic and pulmonary valves are heart valves, not valves within arteries.

old: They have lower pressure, and they have valves to stop the blood flowing backwards.
new: Many veins, especially in the limbs, contain valves that help prevent backflow; not all veins have valves.

old: The wall of a blood vessel has three layers around a central space called the lumen.
new: Large arteries and veins have three principal wall layers surrounding a lumen; capillaries are an important exception.

old: The tunica media is the middle, muscular layer.
new: The tunica media contains smooth muscle and elastic tissue; its thickness varies by vessel type.

old: A normal blood pressure is around one hundred and twenty over eighty millimetres of mercury.
new: A blood pressure near one hundred and twenty over eighty millimetres of mercury is a familiar reference value; diagnostic thresholds vary by guideline and clinical context.

old: Peripheral perfusion means adequate blood flow to the tissues, for example warm hands with a quick capillary refill.
new: Peripheral skin temperature and capillary refill help assess peripheral circulation; a cold limb or delayed refill can be abnormal.

old: A normal saturation is ninety-five to one hundred percent.
new: At sea level, oxygen saturation in most healthy adults is approximately ninety-five to one hundred percent; interpretation depends on clinical context and altitude.

old: Hypertension is high blood pressure, one hundred and thirty over eighty or above.
new: According to the 2025 American Heart Association and American College of Cardiology guideline, hypertension begins at an average systolic pressure of one hundred and thirty or diastolic pressure of eighty millimetres of mercury, based on repeated accurate measurements. Other guidelines use different thresholds.

old: A murmur is an extra or unusual heart sound.
new: A murmur is a sound produced by turbulent blood flow and may be physiological or pathological.

old: Dyspnea is difficult or short breath.
new: Dyspnea is the subjective experience of breathing discomfort, often described as shortness of breath.

old: The stress test shows how the heart responds to exercise.
new: A cardiac stress test evaluates the heart under physical exercise or pharmacological stress.

old: Cardiac markers are blood tests: troponin shows heart muscle injury, C K M B shows muscle damage, and B N P is raised in heart failure.
new: Cardiac troponin indicates myocardial injury but a raised value alone does not establish myocardial infarction. C K M B has a limited contemporary role. B N P and N T pro B N P can support evaluation of heart failure.

old: troponin is one of the most important tests in the emergency department for diagnosing a heart attack.
new: serial high-sensitivity troponin testing, combined with symptoms and ECG findings, is central to evaluating possible acute myocardial infarction.

old: In angioplasty, also called P T C A, a balloon opens a narrowed artery.
new: Angioplasty widens a narrowed vessel, often with a balloon. P T C A specifically means percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty.

old: For clots, anticoagulants inhibit clotting, antiplatelets block the platelets, and thrombolytics dissolve clots that have already formed.
new: For thrombosis prevention and treatment, anticoagulants inhibit coagulation, antiplatelet medicines reduce platelet activation or aggregation, and thrombolytics can dissolve selected established clots.

old: Pneumo and pulmono mean lung or air, as in pneumonia.
new: Pneumo can refer to air or the lung, while pulmono refers to the lung; pneumonia is infection and inflammation of lung tissue.

old: Apnea is a temporary stop in breathing.
new: Apnea is cessation of airflow or breathing; it may be brief or prolonged.

old: And pleuritis is inflamed pleura.
new: Pleuritis is inflammation of the pleura, often causing pain with breathing.

old: Around the nose are the four paranasal sinuses: the frontal, the ethmoidal, the sphenoidal and the maxillary sinuses.
new: There are four groups of paired paranasal sinuses: frontal, ethmoidal air cells, sphenoidal and maxillary.
reason: Four pairs/groups not four individual sinuses

old: Clubbing is enlargement of the fingertips.
new: Clubbing is bulbous enlargement of the distal fingers with changes in nail curvature and the nail-bed angle.

old: Tachypnea is fast breathing, above twenty breaths per minute, and bradypnea is slow breathing, below twelve.
new: For a resting adult, tachypnea commonly refers to a respiratory rate above twenty per minute, while bradypnea is an unusually slow respiratory rate; thresholds vary with age and clinical state.

old: Asthma is reversible narrowing of the airways.
new: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory airway disease with variable respiratory symptoms and variable expiratory airflow limitation.
reason: Do not imply every case is fully reversible

old: Apnea is a temporary absence of breathing.
new: Apnea is an episode of absent breathing or airflow, with variable duration.

old: The respiratory rate is the number of breaths per minute, normally twelve to twenty.
new: Respiratory rate is measured in breaths per minute. Around twelve to twenty at rest is a common adult reference interval, not a universal range for children or illness.

old: Oxygen saturation, or S P O two, is normally ninety-five to one hundred percent.
new: Oxygen saturation, or S P O two, is commonly about ninety-five to one hundred percent in healthy adults at sea level, but targets and expected values depend on the patient and environment.

old: caused by fluid in the alveoli.
new: that may occur with fluid or the sudden opening of small airways.

old: Spirometry measures airflow and lung volumes.
new: Spirometry measures airflow and exhaled volumes such as F E V one and forced vital capacity. It cannot measure residual volume or total lung capacity by itself.

old: And in a pulmonary function test, the patient performs spirometry.
new: Pulmonary function testing includes spirometry and, when indicated, lung volume measurements and diffusing capacity tests.

old: For prefixes: dys, difficult;
new: For prefixes: dys means difficult, painful or abnormal;

old: The esophagus carries food from the pharynx to the stomach.
new: The esophagus carries swallowed food and liquid from the pharynx to the stomach.

old: The small intestine absorbs nutrients, and the large intestine absorbs water.
new: The small intestine absorbs most nutrients and much of the ingested water. The large intestine absorbs remaining water and electrolytes.

old: vomiting is emptying of the stomach through the mouth.
new: vomiting is forceful expulsion of gastric contents through the mouth.

old: And bloating is a feeling of fullness from gas.
new: Bloating is a sense of abdominal fullness or pressure, and abdominal pain is another common digestive symptom.

old: Gastroenteritis is an infection with vomiting and diarrhea: gastro, stomach, entero, intestine, and itis, inflammation.
new: Gastroenteritis is inflammation of the stomach and intestines, often caused by infection, and may produce vomiting and diarrhea: gastro means stomach, entero means intestine, and itis means inflammation.
reason: Not all gastroenteritis must cause both symptoms

old: A barium swallow shows swallowing and the shape of the G I tract on X-ray.
new: A barium swallow examines the pharynx and esophagus during swallowing using fluoroscopic imaging. A broader upper GI barium study may also assess the stomach and duodenum.

old: The pancreatic enzymes measured are amylase, lipase and elastase.
new: Blood lipase and sometimes amylase assist in evaluating acute pancreatic injury; fecal elastase is used to assess exocrine pancreatic insufficiency.

old: A biopsy takes a small tissue sample, and polypectomy is removal of a polyp.
new: A biopsy removes a tissue sample for histological examination, while polypectomy removes a polyp.

old: E R C P examines the bile and pancreatic ducts.
new: E R C P, endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography, uses endoscopy and fluoroscopy to image and often treat disorders of the bile and pancreatic ducts.

old: Paracentesis removes fluid from the abdomen.
new: Paracentesis uses a needle to sample or drain fluid from the peritoneal cavity.

old: And colectomy and appendectomy are removal of the colon and the appendix.
new: Colectomy is surgical removal of part or all of the colon, and appendectomy is removal of the appendix.

old: Proton pump inhibitors and H two blockers reduce acid secretion.
new: Proton pump inhibitors inhibit the gastric H plus K plus A T P ase, whereas H two receptor blockers reduce histamine-stimulated acid secretion.

old: Hepatobiliary drugs support the liver and bile flow.
new: Hepatobiliary treatments depend on the condition; there is no single drug class that generically supports every liver disorder.

old: the urethra removes it.
new: the urethra carries it out of the body.

old: filtration of the blood, regulation of water and salts, homeostasis, storage of urine, and excretion of waste.
new: renal filtration, regulation of fluid, electrolytes and acid-base balance, and excretion of metabolic waste; the urinary bladder stores urine.

old: Anuria is no urine production at all.
new: Anuria is extremely low or essentially absent urine output, often defined clinically as less than one hundred millilitres in twenty-four hours in an adult.

old: Kidney stones are hard mineral deposits that form in the kidney.
new: Urinary stones are hard mineral deposits that may form in the kidney and lodge elsewhere in the urinary tract.

old: benign prostatic hyperplasia is an enlarged prostate that blocks urine flow in older men.
new: benign prostatic hyperplasia is non-cancerous prostate enlargement that can cause bladder outlet obstruction, especially in older men.

old: A urine culture identifies the bacteria causing an infection.
new: A urine culture can identify and quantify organisms growing in urine and, when indicated, support antimicrobial susceptibility testing; results require clinical interpretation.

old: Blood tests measure creatinine, B U N, which is blood urea nitrogen, and the e G F R, the estimated glomerular filtration rate, which tells us how well the kidneys are working.
new: Serum creatinine and urea nitrogen are measured in blood, while e G F R is estimated from creatinine, sometimes with cystatin C, together with factors such as age and sex.

old: And mammo means the breast, as in mammogram.
new: And mammo and masto both refer to the breast, as in mammogram and mastectomy.

old: The female cycle lasts about twenty-eight days, and two cycles run together.
new: The menstrual cycle commonly lasts about twenty-eight days, but normal adult cycles vary, often around twenty-four to thirty-eight days, and ovarian and uterine phases occur in parallel.

old: Around day fourteen is ovulation.
new: In a twenty-eight-day example, ovulation occurs around day fourteen, but its timing varies with cycle length.

old: Infertility means being unable to conceive.
new: Clinically, infertility generally refers to failure to achieve pregnancy after twelve months of regular unprotected intercourse, with earlier evaluation appropriate in some circumstances.

old: Galactorrhea is milk flow that is not from breastfeeding.
new: Galactorrhea is milk-like nipple discharge unrelated to normal pregnancy or breastfeeding.

old: Erectile dysfunction is being unable to keep an erection.
new: Erectile dysfunction is persistent difficulty achieving or maintaining an erection sufficient for satisfactory sexual activity.

old: Polycystic ovary syndrome, P C O S, has many small cysts on the ovaries, with hormone imbalance.
new: Polycystic ovary syndrome, or P C O S, is a heterogeneous endocrine-metabolic disorder. Diagnosis may involve ovulatory dysfunction, hyperandrogenism and polycystic ovarian morphology; ovarian cysts are not required.

old: Endometriosis means endometrial tissue growing outside the uterus.
new: Endometriosis is the presence of endometrium-like tissue outside the uterus.

old: Pelvic inflammatory disease is an infection of the pelvic organs.
new: Pelvic inflammatory disease is infection and inflammation of the upper female genital tract, including the uterus, tubes or nearby tissues.

old: And cervical cancer is an abnormal growth of cervical cells, which screening can detect early.
new: Cervical cancer is a malignant tumor of the cervix, strongly associated with persistent high-risk H P V infection; screening detects precancerous changes and some early cancers.

old: Hormone tests measure F S H, L H, estradiol and testosterone.
new: Hormone testing may include F S H, L H, estradiol, progesterone, testosterone and prolactin, selected according to the clinical question and cycle phase.

old: Hysteroscopy views the inside of the uterus, and colposcopy views the cervix.
new: Hysteroscopy views the uterine cavity, while colposcopy examines the cervix and often the vagina or vulva with magnification.

old: Laparoscopy is surgery through small holes using small instruments.
new: Laparoscopy is a minimally invasive surgical or diagnostic procedure using an endoscope inserted through small abdominal incisions.

old: salpingectomy removes a fallopian tube;
new: salpingectomy removes a uterine or fallopian tube;

old: Hormonal contraceptives prevent ovulation.
new: Hormonal contraceptives prevent pregnancy through various mechanisms, including suppression of ovulation and changes to cervical mucus or the endometrium, depending on the formulation.

old: G n R H analogs suppress L H and F S H.
new: Continuous G n R H agonist treatment eventually suppresses L H and F S H after an initial flare; G n R H antagonists inhibit their release directly.

old: Hirsutism is excess body or facial hair.
new: Hirsutism is excessive terminal hair growth in a male-pattern distribution in females.

old: Dwarfism is abnormally short stature, and gigantism is excessive growth, both related to growth hormone in childhood.
new: Short stature has many possible causes, not all related to growth hormone deficiency. Gigantism refers to excessive growth due to growth hormone excess before epiphyseal closure.

old: Hyperthyroidism is excess thyroid hormone, and hypothyroidism is reduced thyroid hormone.
new: Hyperthyroidism is increased synthesis and secretion of thyroid hormones by the gland; thyrotoxicosis is the clinical state of thyroid hormone excess from any cause. Hypothyroidism means insufficient thyroid hormone action.

old: Type one diabetes is an autoimmune destruction of the beta cells, so the body makes no insulin.
new: Type one diabetes usually involves autoimmune loss of pancreatic beta cells, leading to severe insulin deficiency; residual secretion may remain early in disease.

old: Type two diabetes is caused by insulin resistance, and it is much more common.
new: Type two diabetes results from insulin resistance together with progressive beta-cell dysfunction and is the most common form.

old: And pancreatic N E Ts, neuroendocrine tumors, are hormone-secreting tumors.
new: Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors may be functional and secrete hormones, or nonfunctional without a clinically important hormone syndrome.

old: Myelo is the spinal cord, as in myelitis.
new: Myelo can mean spinal cord or bone marrow depending on context; myelitis is inflammation of the spinal cord and myelopoiesis means marrow blood-cell formation.

old: Thymo means mind or emotion, as in dysthymia, a long-lasting low mood.
new: In psychiatric terminology, thym-o refers to mood or emotion, as in dysthymia. In other contexts, thym-o refers to the thymus gland; always interpret the term in context.

old: Vertigo is a spinning feeling, or imbalance.
new: Vertigo is an illusory sensation of self-motion or environmental motion, commonly spinning; imbalance without perceived motion is not necessarily vertigo.

old: A stroke is blocked blood flow to the brain.
new: Stroke is an acute neurological injury caused by disrupted cerebral blood flow, either by arterial blockage, called ischemic stroke, or by bleeding, called hemorrhagic stroke.

old: Epilepsy means recurrent seizures.
new: Epilepsy is a brain disorder characterized by an enduring predisposition to generate unprovoked seizures; recurrent unprovoked seizures are a common presentation.

old: In the cognitive group, dementia is a gradual memory loss, while delirium is acute confusion.
new: Major neurocognitive disorder, often called dementia, involves acquired cognitive decline affecting independence; memory may be affected but is not always the main symptom. Delirium is an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness.

old: Anemia means a lack of blood.
new: Anemia means hemoglobin concentration below the expected reference threshold for age, sex or physiological state; it does not simply mean lack of blood.

old: and thymo is the thymus, as in thymectomy.
new: and in this anatomical context thym-o refers to the thymus, as in thymectomy, rather than the psychiatric root relating to mood.

old: Platelets, or thrombocytes, help clotting, which we call hemostasis.
new: Platelets participate in primary hemostasis; hemostasis also includes vascular responses and the coagulation cascade, followed by fibrinolysis.

old: group O has neither the A nor the B antigen.
new: group O has neither A nor B antigens on the red cells, although other red-cell antigens remain present.
reason: Group O does not have zero RBC antigens

old: Pallor is pale skin from low hemoglobin.
new: Pallor is reduced visible skin or mucosal coloration and may be associated with anemia, vasoconstriction or reduced peripheral perfusion.

old: Anemia is a low oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood.
new: Anemia is hemoglobin below the appropriate reference limit, often reducing the oxygen-carrying capacity of blood.

old: And D I C, disseminated intravascular coagulation, is widespread clotting throughout the blood vessels.
new: Disseminated intravascular coagulation involves systemic activation of coagulation with microvascular thrombosis and consumption of platelets and clotting factors, so bleeding and organ dysfunction may also occur.

old: describe the main parts of the skin, the eye, the ear, the tongue and the nose.
new: describe the main structures of the skin, eye and ear, while recognizing basic terminology of smell and taste.

old: The skin has three layers.
new: The diagram shows three regions: epidermis, dermis and the hypodermis. Strictly speaking, the skin proper consists of the epidermis and dermis; the hypodermis is subcutaneous tissue beneath it.

old: Dermo and cutaneo both mean skin, as in dermatology and cutaneous.
new: Derm-o, dermat-o and cutane-o all refer to skin, as in dermatology and cutaneous.

old: A macule is a flat spot, like a freckle.
new: A macule is a flat, nonpalpable area of altered color usually less than one centimetre across, such as a freckle. A larger flat lesion is commonly called a patch.

old: A nodule is a solid, deeper lesion.
new: A nodule is a solid, palpable lesion, often larger than one centimetre and extending into the dermis or subcutis.

old: Patch testing identifies allergic contact.
new: Patch testing helps identify delayed-type contact allergens in suspected allergic contact dermatitis.

old: A Wood's lamp uses ultraviolet light to detect certain infections.
new: A Wood's lamp uses ultraviolet light to support the assessment of selected infections and pigmentary changes, but it is not a definitive test on its own.

old: Lacrimo means the tear gland, as in lacrimal duct.
new: Lacrim-o refers to tears or the lacrimal apparatus, as in the lacrimal gland and lacrimal duct.

old: Vestibulo refers to balance, as in vestibulitis.
new: Vestibul-o refers to the vestibule of the inner ear, involved in balance, as in vestibulocochlear nerve.

old: Olfacto means smell, as in olfaction, and osmo means odour or smell.
new: Olfact-o and osm-o refer to smell, as in olfaction and anosmia, the loss of smell. Osm-o should not be confused with the unrelated osmosis.

old: Glaucoma is raised pressure inside the eye that damages the optic nerve.
new: Glaucoma is a group of progressive optic neuropathies, often associated with increased intraocular pressure, but it can occur with pressure in the normal range.

old: For taste, with the root geusia:
new: For taste, using the combining form geus-i or the suffix geusia:

old: LASIK uses a laser to reshape the cornea and correct vision.
new: L A S I K stands for laser-assisted in situ keratomileusis. It uses a laser to reshape the cornea and correct selected refractive errors.

old: Ophthalmic antibiotics treat eye infections, and ophthalmic anesthetics numb the eye surface.
new: Ophthalmic antibiotics treat bacterial eye infections when indicated, not viral or noninfectious eye disorders; topical ophthalmic anesthetics numb the eye surface for procedures.
